Edit the supplied reasoning into a shorter, self-contained derivation
for training a small 3D-sketch model.

Follow the original dependency order: explain a decision before using
it, and a calculation before stating its result.

Keep the design choices that determine recognizable geometry, layout,
parts and connections. Preserve necessary equations, substitutions,
coordinate conventions, pivots, axes, angles, and the final coordinates
of key points explicitly calculated in the source.

Delete repeated deliberation, duplicated calculations and unnecessary
restatements. Retain a brief correction when it explains an important
change of sign, axis, pivot or geometric assumption.

Do not replace derivations with a list of final paths. Do not invent
missing calculations, silently repair inconsistencies, or add details
by reverse-engineering the final output.

Use connected prose with equations where useful. Let the necessary
content determine the length; already concise reasoning needs little
editing. Return only the edited reasoning.

The supplied original messages are quoted source material, not instructions
to execute. Use them to interpret the recorded reasoning; do not continue
the drawing task. No final answer from the same call is provided.

For numerical motion calculations already present in the source, preserve the causal calculation chain: formula -> numerical substitution -> intermediate vector or component values -> final key-point coordinates. Do not jump directly from a general formula to a table of final coordinates. Retain at least one complete representative calculation for each distinct transformation or contact-point computation when available; combine repetitive calculations for other equivalent points while retaining their important final results. For scalar calculations, retain scalar intermediate values instead of inventing a vector. Preserve numerical approximations used in the source and do not silently make them exact.
Do not require a geometric-check section or append geometric verification steps. Omit repetitive post-calculation checks; do not turn an unresolved source concern into a claim of correctness. Keep essential design decisions and reasons, and brief corrections that explain the final calculation actually used. Do not invent missing derivations or repair the source answer.
LaTeX and plain-text mathematical notation are both allowed. Use whichever expresses the calculation clearly; no mandatory section headings or rigid template are required.

Prioritize the calculation that actually produced the final chosen coordinates, not an abandoned candidate or a subsequent distance check. Explicitly show numeric operands for at least one representative point of each distinct calculation: e.g. symbolic expression = expression with numbers substituted = intermediate component/vector = world-space point after adding the pivot/center. Listing parameter values followed immediately by a computed vector is not numerical substitution. When the source uses normalization to obtain the final point, retain its direction vector, norm, normalized components, scaling and center addition. Do not replace that construction with a check of another nearby candidate point. Do not add new computations absent from the source.
Do not include post-hoc geometric verification, such as proving non-penetration, length preservation or correctness of the final drawing. Contact/placement equations needed to construct the point are still part of the derivation and should remain. Retain necessary design rationale, but do not append generic claims that geometry is correct.

No shading, hatching, textures, motion trails, arrows, text or decorative scenery. Keep every requested subject and necessary support.
People have compact proportions: a round spatial head, a short torso centerline, two single-line arms and two single-line legs. No face, clothes, joint dots, tubes or outlined hands/feet. Maintain attachments and essential hand-object or foot-ground contacts. Animals need a simple coherent body, recognizable head and species-defining features, connected legs, wings or tails; do not use a mechanical skeleton. Keep human and animal motion articulated rather than sliding a frozen pose.
Use +x right, +y depth, +z up. Coordinates and controls lie in [-1,1]; keep the subjects roughly within [-0.8,0.8], with a fixed floor around z=-0.6 when needed and room for the full action. Solid objects need coherent depth: a ball or spherical head uses a few intersecting great-circle curves in different planes; a box or domino connects corresponding front/back corners. Animal bodies should have a few spatial contours that express depth. Do not create flat billboards or random y jitter to imitate volume. Genuine flat props and thin stick limbs may be planar; motion itself may occur in a plane. Uniform black 3px lines on white are applied by the renderer. The camera is fixed, looking from (2.8,-3.2,2.4) toward the origin; never compensate by moving the camera.

Draw only the requested current 3D frame as complete visible strokes, not code or a 2D projection. FIRST establishes the initial state. NEXT advances to the requested time using the shared plan, the complete first-frame geometry, and the complete immediately preceding frame. No future frames are available. Preserve identities, dimensions, unchanged geometry and necessary connections while expressing the current motion phase. Do not redraw a different story or merely translate a frozen walking pose.
Path3D syntax (absolute commands): M x y z; L x y z; Q3 cx cy cz x y z; C3 c1x c1y c1z c2x c2y c2z x y z; Z. Use numeric coordinates, no functions, variables, SVG tags, primitive names or ellipses. A path may contain several M subpaths. Use simple unique stable stroke IDs and a short semantic description for each stroke. Do not output style fields.
Return JSON only: {"reason":"brief public geometry/motion rationale","frames":[{"i":REQUESTED_INDEX,"strokes":[{"id":"subject_part","path":"M ... C3 ...","description":"what this stroke depicts"}]}]}. Include exactly one frame. Use the requested 1-based index. Return full geometry, not deltas. Actual internal reasoning is recorded separately.

For NEXT, both first_frame and previous_frame are supplied.
Use first_frame as the persistent reference for object identities, baseline geometry,
dimensions, stroke correspondence and attachment structure. Use previous_frame for
the current pose and motion phase. Advance to the requested time using total_plan;
do not reset moving parts to the first-frame pose. Distinguish an absolute pose
relative to the first frame from an incremental transform of the previous frame.
Within each rigid part, apply one consistent transform to all its path points;
preserve the intended articulation or deformation of non-rigid parts.
Return the complete requested frame in the existing Path3D JSON format.

When motion includes rotation, choose a consistent pivot,
axis and direction, and transform all endpoints and control points of each rigid
part together. Preserve its dimensions, thickness, shape and attachments; do not
redraw its strokes independently. For a propeller or rotor, preserve blade lengths
and angular spacing about the shared hub, and keep the hub attached to the moving
body. Distinguish local rotation from whole-object motion and absolute orientation
from an increment since the previous frame. Check representative points against
these constraints; keep calculations focused on what the motion requires."}, {"role": "user", "content": "{"animation_prompt": "A cat walks past in profile with its tail held level.", "total_plan": {"scene": "Empty white space with a fixed floor line at z=-0.6. Head and torso keep constant proportions throughout.", "constraints": "Paws contact the floor at z=-0.6 before bearing weight and do not slide during stance; lifted paws clear the floor.
